Last semester, Professor Jomon stopped me after class with my essay in his hand. "This section on labour markets reads differently. Which parts did a tool help with?"
I opened my mouth and nothing came out. I honestly didn't know. I'd used a chatbot to explain a few terms, then to smooth some paragraphs, then to suggest a structure, and I hadn't kept track of any of it. He wasn't accusing me, but I couldn't prove what was mine.
That evening I made a simple log in my notebook: date, assignment, what I asked the tool, what I kept. On the next essay I added two lines at the end: "An AI tool was used to explain two concepts and check grammar. All analysis is my own." 
Professor Jomon read it and nodded. That was Irawati, finally able to answer the question.

qa.q: What did Irawati record in the new log?
qa.a: The date, the assignment, what Irawati asked the tool, and what was kept.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel when Professor Jomon asked which parts a tool helped with?
qa.a: Irawati felt flustered and exposed, unable to say anything because no track had been kept of what was really their own.

qa.q: What else could Irawati do to make the disclosure more useful?
qa.a: Irawati could ask the professor what level of detail the course expects, so the acknowledgment matches the rules instead of guessing.

qa.q: How might Professor Jomon see the change on the next essay?
qa.a: Professor Jomon likely feels reassured, since the acknowledgment answers the question he had asked and makes trust easier.

grounding: Shows a student who, after a professor's question, starts logging AI use and adds an acknowledgment, making clear which work is their own.

subtype: Approach: add disclosure and keep a record of use [Revision]

Note, seminar course, week 9. Written by Francis, course tutor.
In week 6 I asked Rehana why two paragraphs of her report used terms we hadn't covered. She looked down, said she'd asked a chatbot to "tidy" her draft, and wasn't sure how much it had changed. She seemed embarrassed rather than defensive.
I explained that the course allows tools for some tasks but expects students to say where. I didn't mark her down.
This week she handed in her essay with a one-page record stapled to the back: each time she used the tool, what she asked, and what she kept or threw away. At the end of the essay she wrote a short acknowledgment. Her own paragraphs were rougher but clearer about her argument.
Next step: I've asked her if I can show her record format, without her name, to the rest of the group.

qa.q: What did Rehana staple to the back of her essay?
qa.a: A one-page record of each time she used the tool, what she asked, and what she kept or threw away.

qa.q: How did Rehana seem to feel when first asked about the paragraphs?
qa.a: She seemed embarrassed rather than defensive, looking down and admitting she was not sure how much the tool had changed.

qa.q: What else could the tutor do to help the whole group?
qa.a: Sharing a simple record format with everyone would make disclosure normal, so no student has to guess what to write.

qa.q: How might other students in the group see Rehana's record if it is shared?
qa.a: Other students might feel relieved to have a clear example of how to disclose tool use without fear of being marked down.

grounding: Shows a student, after a tutor's question, beginning to record AI use and add an acknowledgment, which protects trust in her work.
